DOCUMENT S08 — Rail fleet and service records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) fleet technical review; rail accounts as published by the
Office of Rail and Road (ORR), National Grid ESO, Ofgem and the E3C; roles only, no individuals
Record type: reconstructed fleet and service-impact records, each part restating one published account
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: clock times are as printed, with no clock labelled (GTR prints "1653", ORR "around
4:52pm"); read as BST (UTC+01:00) because ESO dates the event at 4:52pm. Durations are as each source states.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated by the named source; [estimated] value the source gives as
approximate ("circa", "approximately", "around", "c."); [measured], [modelled], [digitised] and
[illustrative] not used. Each part restates one published account in its own terms.

PART 1 — GTR TECHNICAL REVIEW ("Power Surge Disruption on 9th August 2019: Technical Review", dated 3
September 2019; provided by GTR to the ESO and appended to the ESO technical report as Appendix F)
G01  Event summary 1: from information supplied by the National Grid at 1653 [reported] on Friday 9 August,
     the frequency of the OLE AC voltage supply dropped below 49 Hz [reported] for 16 seconds [reported]; it
     dropped below 48.89 Hz [reported] to a minimum of 48.8 Hz [reported] for milliseconds.
G02  Event summary 2: there was no identified OLE AC voltage supply interruption.
G03  Event summary 3: all Desiro City Class 700 and 717 units operating on AC voltage suffered a Protective
     Shutdown, in which the converter known as the 4QC (4 Quadrant Controller) shut down. No other AC trains
     in the GTR fleet suffered power-related issues from the event (e.g. Class 387, Class 365, Class 313).
G04  Event summary 4: in passenger service this involved circa 60 [estimated] units, Class 700 FLU/RLUs and
     Class 717, suffering a 4QC lock out.
G05  Event summary 5: with the 4QC shut down the train switches to battery power: loss of HVAC (fan-only fresh
     air supply), standby reduced lighting (emergency lighting activates when battery voltage drops), no
     at-seat power, no PIS displays (audio only from the cab) and no traction power. The GSM-R radio remains
     active.
G06  Event summary 6: after failed attempts to repower the trains, the established first response for a train
     failing with these symptoms is for the driver to reboot the train, known as a Battery Reset, which takes
     approximately 10 minutes [estimated].
G07  Event summary 7: Fleet Control diagnosed the issue quickly and a global GSM-R call was broadcast
     instructing drivers to carry out the Battery Reset process.
G08  Event summary 8: after this, 27 [reported] of the affected units were recovered.
G09  Event summary 9: the remaining circa 30 [estimated] units required the Protective Shutdown to be unlocked
     by a technician with a laptop attending each unit.
G10  Event summary 10: 17 [reported] technicians were available at the time of the event; they were sent
     immediately to stranded units with laptops, and a further 24 [reported] technicians were mobilised within
     the next hour. The affected trains were widely spread geographically and some were not easily accessible.
G11  Event summary 11: the process took some time and resulted in 23 [reported] train evacuations and severe
     levels of service disruption.
G12  Cause 1: the Desiro City from Siemens Mobility is a software-enabled commuter train and requires
     protection against power supply frequency excursions, for safety reasons and to protect low power
     electronics.
G13  Cause 2: the Siemens technical specification for the train states that it will continue to operate with
     supply frequency drops down to 48.5 Hz [reported] for short periods of time.
G14  Cause 3: the NR Electrification System Compatibility document NR/GN/ELP/27010 ("Guidance for
     compatibility between electric trains and electrification systems"), a Manufacturing and Supply Agreement
     compliance requirement, identifies that the supply frequency can fall to 48.5 Hz [reported] in extreme
     conditions.
G15  Cause 4: a review of the Class 700 NoBo design submission (Siemens document A6Z00036309602 item
     4.2.8.2.2) shows that compliance with both NR/GN/ELP 27010 and EN 50163 would be demonstrated.
G16  Cause 5: Siemens advised that the train's supply frequency response was designed to comply with EN 50163
     Clause 4.2 Note 2, which permits train drives to disconnect at 49 Hz [reported]; using this value in the
     design led the train to shut down its drives protectively when the supply frequency fell below
     49 Hz [reported].
G17  Cause 6: Siemens also clarified that there should not have been a Permanent Lockout following a
     protective shutdown caused by a supply frequency drop; all trains should have been recoverable by Battery
     Reset, whereas 30 [reported] trains were not recoverable. This was not the intended behaviour of the
     train.
G18  Cause 7: the affected Class 700 and 717 sets therefore did not react according to their design intent in
     these circumstances; the risk of this happening was not known before the power event on Friday 9 August.
G19  Cause 8: separately, the new TCMS (Train Control Management System) software version 3.27 removed the
     driver's ability to recover from a Permanent Lockout by using the Battery Reset process.
G20  Cause 9: on 9 August all units that required a technician to recover power were at software level 3.27 or
     above; the 28 [reported] units recovered by the driver performing a Battery Reset were at the previous
     TCMS software level of 3.25 or below.
G21  Conclusion 1: all Class 700 and Class 717 trains operating on AC suffered a Protective Shutdown of the
     4QC controller because of a drop in the supply frequency below 49 Hz [reported] for
     16 seconds [reported].
G22  Conclusion 2 to 4: this was not how the train system had been specified to operate, and the event should
     not have caused a Permanent Lockout fault. The effects were exacerbated because the fleet was undergoing
     a software change that removed the Battery Reset remedy for Permanent Lockout events, so the driver could
     not recover failed trains operating on the new software and a technician was required to attend.
G23  Planned mitigation 1: Siemens are developing a software patch to allow units that protectively shut down
     below 49 Hz [reported] supply frequency to recover themselves, without a reboot or laptop, when the
     frequency rises above 49.5 Hz [reported].
G24  Planned mitigation 2: neither Siemens nor GTR proposes to revert units to previous software versions,
     because of concerns about unit availability; based on discussions with the National Grid Head of
     Networks, the risk of a frequency excursion below 49 Hz [reported] before the patch is fully introduced
     is considered extremely unlikely.
G25  Planned mitigation 3: Siemens will also investigate how the train could be made to operate for a short
     time with the supply frequency falling to 48.5 Hz [reported].

PART 2 — ESO TECHNICAL REPORT (dated 6 September 2019): rail passages of section 5.2, the executive summary
and section 7
E01  ESO 5.2: Class 700 and 717 trains shut down north of Farringdon and Kings Cross stations because their
     internal protection systems were triggered; the Network Rail overhead line power supply operated
     continually. The shutdown delayed all other trains behind them, requiring the temporary closure of London
     St Pancras and Kings Cross stations, which led to Friday rush-hour overcrowding.
E02  ESO 5.2, summarising GTR's report: all Desiro City Class 700 and Class 717 trains operating on AC power
     suffered a protective shutdown when the frequency deviation fell below 49 Hz [reported]. Of the
     approximately 60 [estimated] trains that shut down, half were restarted by the driver on site performing
     a reboot, which takes c. 10 minutes [estimated]; the remaining 30 [reported] trains required a technician
     to attend each train with a laptop to reset it.
E03  ESO 5.2: GTR stated that this was not how the train system had been specified to operate and that the
     event should not have caused a permanent lockout fault; the trains' technical specification states that
     they will continue to operate with supply frequency drops down to 48.5 Hz [reported] for short periods.
     All other GTR classes of train were unaffected.
E04  ESO 5.2: the effects were exacerbated because the fleet was undergoing a software change, which meant
     drivers could not recover trains operating on the new software. Siemens are developing a patch to let
     drivers recover the trains themselves without a reboot or a technician attending, and will investigate
     how the train could operate for a short time with a supply frequency of 48.5 Hz [reported].
E05  ESO 5.2: the impact on the rail network was 23 [reported] train evacuations, and thousands of passengers
     had their journeys delayed, with 371 [reported] trains cancelled, 220 [reported] part cancelled and
     873 [reported] trains delayed. London St Pancras and King's Cross stations had to close for several hours
     due to overcrowding, and London Euston went exit only for a period of time.
E06  Executive summary: a major contributor to the rail disruption was a particular class of train operating
     in the South-East: approximately 60 [estimated] trains unexpectedly shut down when the frequency dropped
     below 49 Hz [reported], half of which required a visit from a technician to restart.
E07  ESO section 7 (report findings): disruption to rail services extended through Friday evening and into
     Saturday morning because approximately 30 [estimated] trains stopped operating and could not be restarted
     following the original frequency drop to 49 Hz [reported]; restarting them required a technician with a
     laptop to attend each train, which took some time.

PART 3 — ORR REPORT ("Report following railway power disruption on 9th August 2019", dated 3 January 2020)
O01  ORR 1.0: on Friday 9 August 2019 around 4:52pm [reported] a number of generators tripped off the power
     grid at approximately the same time. The frequency of the power supply to the rail network dropped from
     its nominal 50.0 Hz [reported] to below 49.0 Hz [reported] for approximately 33 seconds [estimated],
     falling to a low of 48.8 Hz [reported]. The majority of rolling stock operated without any issues.
O02  ORR 1.0: 31 [reported] trains were stranded as a result of the temporary drop in frequency. On the Class
     700 and Class 717 rolling stock, protection systems operated within 200 ms [reported] of the frequency
     falling to 49.0 Hz [reported], causing a lock-out of 29 [reported] trains: 22 [reported] trains were
     permanently locked out and could not be reset without a technician attending on site, while 7 [reported]
     trains were restored through driver reset. Two Class 387 trains were also trapped as a result of the
     lock-out of the Class 700 and Class 717 trains. Passengers had to be evacuated (detrained) from
     30 [reported] trains to a place of safety, and there were substantial knock-on delays following recovery
     of the vehicles.
O03  ORR 2.1: the supplied power frequency dropped from a nominal 50.0 Hz [reported] to a low of
     48.8 Hz [reported] after 16 seconds [reported]; it remained below 49.0 Hz [reported] for approximately
     33 seconds [estimated] and was restored to its nominal 50 Hz [reported] 3 minutes and
     36 seconds [reported] later. ORR's Figure 1 (not reproduced here) is a frequency trace captioned as
     extracted from the National Grid technical report "published 06/08/2019".
O04  ORR 2.1: the majority of rolling stock operated without notable issues, but a fleet of Class 700 and
     Class 717 trains operated by GTR shut down within 200 ms [reported] of the frequency dropping below
     49.0 Hz [reported].
O05  ORR 2.2: within 200 ms [reported] of the supply frequency dropping below 49.0 Hz [reported],
     29 [reported] trains comprising Class 700 and Class 717, operated by GTR, shut down and were locked out
     by on-board safety systems. Initial attempts by drivers to bring the trains back into operation proved
     abortive, and Fleet Control had to advise drivers on the next action.
O06  ORR 2.2: ORR quotes GTR's technical review that all Desiro City Class 700 and 717 units operating on AC
     voltage suffered a Protective Shutdown in which the converter, known as the 4QC (expanded by ORR as Four
     Quadrant Chopper), shut down. When the 4QC shuts down the train is isolated from the traction power
     supply; only the limited on-board battery supply remains, which powers certain key systems but not
     traction.
O07  ORR 2.2: after Fleet Control diagnosed the shutdown, a GSM-R call was broadcast instructing drivers of
     affected trains to carry out the Battery Reset Process, which recovered 7 [reported] of the affected
     units; 22 [reported] trains could not be reset and required a technician to attend to recover them.
O08  ORR 2.2: at the time of the event too few technicians were available for the number of stranded trains;
     18 [reported] technicians with laptops were sent to restore the trains immediately, and more technicians
     were mobilised within the next hour.
O09  ORR 2.3: some trains were in locations that were not easily accessible, which made recovery
     time-consuming. Passengers were safely detrained at stations and on track from 30 [reported] stranded
     trains. There were significant delays, cancellations and part-cancellations of train journeys; full
     service was restored within 24 hours [reported].
O10  ORR 2.3, Table 1 "Affected routes, cancellations and delays" (source printed by ORR: Network Rail's
     National Daily Report 09/08/2019). Columns: route | cancelled | part-cancelled | delay minutes
T1   Sussex | 38 [reported] | 22 [reported] | 2051 [reported]
T2   Wessex | 0 [reported] | 2 [reported] | 716 [reported]
T3   Kent | 36 [reported] | 43 [reported] | 1727 [reported]
T4   Western | 0 [reported] | 0 [reported] | 658 [reported]
T5   LNE-York | 86 [reported] | 44 [reported] | 5569 [reported]
T6   LNE-EM | 197 [reported] | 79 [reported] | 2780 [reported]
T7   LNW-N | 14 [reported] | 24 [reported] | 428 [reported]
T8   Wales | 0 [reported] | 6 [reported] | 499 [reported]
T9   TOTAL | 371 [reported] | 220 [reported] | 14428 [reported]
O11  ORR 2.5: delay compensation claims received by train operators in period 5 (21 July to 18 August) rose to
     the highest level since the May 2018 timetable disruption, with a particular peak for GTR; ORR states
     this cannot be directly attributed to the power disruption but is likely to have been a factor. There was
     no corresponding peak in complaints.
O12  ORR 3.0: ORR engaged with Network Rail, GTR and Siemens to understand why the power disruption
     significantly affected railway services despite traction power not being lost. Network Rail owns and
     manages the infrastructure; GTR operates the affected trains and carries out some of the maintenance;
     Siemens, the manufacturer, designed the software on the affected trains and also maintains some of the
     trains.
O13  ORR 3.1: ORR uses "lock-out" for a situation where a component's operation has been stopped by a
     software-based protection system. Permanent lock-outs protect against high-severity on-board risks such
     as fire and electrocution, and need a technician with a laptop to connect physically to the train to
     reset them. Temporary lock-outs protect against low-severity risks after a short-lived fault or
     mal-operation: the train resets itself once the fault clears, or the driver resets the software using a
     Battery Reset Process.
O14  ORR 3.1: all Class 700 and 717 trains had been programmed by Siemens to operate from a nominal
     50.0 Hz [reported] supply with a minimum frequency of 49.0 Hz [reported]. When the software detected that
     the frequency had dropped below this level it operated as designed, disconnecting the traction drive
     within 200 ms [reported].
O15  ORR 3.1: individual trains had different software levels installed, as a software change was being
     implemented progressively across the fleets. On detecting the frequency drop, the units with software
     version 3.25.x went into a temporary lock-out while the units with version 3.27.x went into permanent
     lock-out; drivers could reset the temporary lock-outs with a battery reset, while the permanent lock-outs
     required a technician to attend.
O16  ORR 3.2: version 3.27.x was intended to address a safety risk identified with 3.25.x: the TCMS could lock
     out a train system in response to a serious fault or out-of-specification condition, only for the driver
     to clear it with a battery reset and restore power to the fault. Siemens therefore implemented in 3.27.x
     a permanent lock-out that a battery reset could not clear, needing a technician to analyse its cause
     before clearing it; among the trigger conditions selected was the detection of a low power supply
     frequency.
O17  ORR 3.3: the lock-out on out-of-limit supply frequency is understood to protect against electromagnetic
     interference from the 4QC in a range that can affect signalling circuits. ORR states that such protection
     is only required while the supply is outside the specified frequency range, so the lock-out could be
     permitted to reset automatically when the frequency returns to nominal, and that the service-disrupting
     implications of a lock-out needing a driver or technician reset appear not to have been given weight when
     the protection parameters for the on-train software were developed.
O18  ORR 3.3: variations in supply frequency affect many trains at once, with the same response from all
     trains on the same software. ORR states that the collective response of the Class 700 and 717 trains was
     in accordance with the software design but was not an explicit intention, and that Siemens accepts the
     temporary reduction in frequency should not have been considered a situation requiring a permanent
     lock-out.
O19  ORR 3.4: ORR quotes an interim Siemens email: in the original Class 700 design the 4QCs stop pulsing when
     the line frequency is out of range and restart automatically, without driver action, when it comes back
     in range; with the hysteresis implemented, the 4QCs lock when the line frequency drops below
     49 Hz [reported] and restart when it rises above 49.5 Hz [reported].
O20  ORR 4.0 (conclusion): 23 [reported] trains were evacuated without incident. The significant delays could
     be attributed to the permanent lock-out of some of the Class 700 and Class 717 trains; findings so far
     show that the TCMS software classed the frequency reduction as a scenario requiring a permanent lock-out.
O21  ORR 4.0 (conclusion): the permanent lock-out resulted in 30 [reported] trains running the upgraded
     software being effectively stranded on the network and requiring a technician reset, with significant
     knock-on effects beyond the initial incident; full service was restored within 24 hours [reported].
O22  ORR 4.0 (conclusion): so far ORR has not been able to establish any non-compliance with the Railways
     (Interoperability) Regulations 2011, as amended, that could warrant enforcement action; the findings are
     lessons learned to be fed back for awareness and improvement.

PART 4 — RAIL FIGURES IN OTHER PUBLISHED REPORTS
X01  Ofgem report (dated 3 January 2020), 2.6: 29 [reported] GTR Class 700 and 717 trains shut down and became
     stranded when the system frequency fell below 49 Hz [reported], due to their own on-board automatic
     frequency protection systems; two Class 387 trains were also trapped by the stranded units, and
     altogether passengers had to be safely evacuated from 30 [reported] trains.
X02  Ofgem 2.7: some protection settings were reset by the driver, but 22 [reported] permanently locked out
     and had to be reset by a technician, which was the main cause of disruption to rail lines into St Pancras
     International and King's Cross. A software update is being introduced so that these trains can be reset
     automatically if the frequency drops below 49 Hz [reported] in future.
X03  Ofgem 2.9: there was significant disruption to the rail network, with 371 [reported] services cancelled
     and 220 [reported] part cancelled. Ofgem executive summary: rail services were particularly affected,
     with more than 500 [reported] services disrupted.
X04  E3C interim report: the Department for Transport confirmed that a safety mechanism built into all
     operational Class 700 and Class 717 Desiro City trains detected the frequency drop and triggered
     60 [reported] trains to shut down; around half were restarted by their drivers and the rest required
     engineers to be dispatched, blocking tracks into St Pancras International and King's Cross.
     371 [reported] services were cancelled and 873 [reported] delayed, and St Pancras International, King's
     Cross and Euston had to limit passenger numbers entering the stations at various times.
X05  E3C interim report: a number of trains did not end up in their correct location at the end of the day,
     which disrupted some early morning services on Saturday 10 August; the executive summary states that rail
     delays extended into Sunday 11 August. The Class 700 and 717 trains had been introduced over the last
     three years.
X06  E3C final report (January 2020), section 4: Thameslink Class 700 and 717 train systems were
     overprotective to frequency drops and shut down; a number of trains required manual engineer intervention
     to restart, and the complexity of the restart process caused significant disruption: 371 [reported]
     cancelled services, 220 [reported] part cancelled services and 873 [reported] delayed services.

DOCUMENT S11 — Essential services and infrastructure supply impact records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: compiled from the National Grid ESO, Ofgem, E3C and ORR published accounts (DNO, Network
Rail and service-provider statements as those reports give them); roles only, no individuals
Record type: reconstructed impact records by service, each item restating one published account
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: clock times are hh:mm as printed, with no clock labelled; read as BST (UTC+01:00) because
ESO dates the event at 4:52pm. Durations are as each source states them.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the named source; [estimated] value the source gives as
approximate ("approximately", "c.", "~"); [measured], [modelled], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
The two index entries of Part 7 are written for this record; the statement and article they index are not
reproduced.

PART 1 — RAIL AND TRANSPORT POWER SUPPLIES
P01  ESO technical report (dated 6 September 2019), section 5.2: the DNOs confirmed that no track supplies
     were lost due to the DNOs' LFDD protection operation. Through its investigation, Network Rail stated that
     its supply disruption was likely to have been caused by supply interruption from the DNO networks, and is
     to undertake discussions with the DNOs to explore this further.
P02  ESO section 5.2: the built-in resilience of Network Rail's electrical power infrastructure meant traction
     power was maintained to the vast majority of the railway throughout the incident; supply-related trips
     occurred at two DC traction locations, which Network Rail is investigating further. Eight signal power
     supplies, principally in rural locations, suffered minor outages with minimal passenger impact; Network
     Rail is reviewing resilience at these locations with the DNOs.
P03  ESO section 5.2: London Underground confirmed impacts on the Victoria Line, which was suspended as a
     result of the event; service was restored at 17:35 [reported]. UKPN confirmed that LFDD did not affect
     the Victoria line; the UKPN control room contacted London Underground, which confirmed that it did not
     lose power supplies at any stations but had an internal traction issue.
P04  ORR report (dated 3 January 2020), sections 1.0 and 2.4: there was a traction power outage on the Wirral
     line of Merseyrail after rectifiers tripped when domestic supply was lost to LFDD, resulting in
     428 minutes [reported] of delay; in other areas no traction power outage was reported.
P05  ORR section 2.4: the substations at Tattenham and Chipstead experienced power quality issues, which
     caused the protective devices for the traction rectifiers to operate, temporarily switching the power
     off; the rectifiers were quickly reinstated, and traction power supply was maintained during this time.
P06  ORR section 2.4: two DNO supply points were lost, at Chatham and Lewes; ORR states this is still under
     investigation and may have been caused by LFDD.
P07  ORR section 2.4: eight signalling power supplies were lost in rural locations fed by local DNO networks
     that may have been affected by LFDD: Wye (Kent), Southease (Sussex), Norwood Fork (London), Trowbridge
     (Wiltshire), Magor (Wales), Bangor (Wales), Croes Newydd (Wales) and Kirby Thore (Cumbria).
     Investigations are ongoing into whether the power disruption led to the loss of these supplies.
P08  ORR section 4.0 (conclusion): Network Rail's electrical system reacted well although some resilience
     issues were identified; Network Rail has begun work to ensure adequate back-up supplies for non-traction
     essential supplies where necessary and is working with the DNO to improve resilience.
P09  Ofgem report (dated 3 January 2020), 2.8: the traction supplies to the Wirral line on Merseyrail were
     disconnected as a result of SP Energy Networks' LFDD operations. Three Transport for London stations and
     eight signalling sites at rural locations across England and Wales were also thought to have been
     affected by LFDD operations, although traction supplies were unaffected.
P10  E3C final report (January 2020), section 4: power supplies to the local Wirral Line were interrupted by
     the LFDD scheme, causing a 428 minute [reported] delay for passengers. Three Transport for London
     stations were disconnected as a result of LFDD operations; traction supplies to these sites were
     maintained, with minimal impact on passengers.
P11  E3C final report, section 4: eight rail signalling assets were affected, principally in rural locations
     across England and Wales, with minimal customer impact; 2 [reported] were disconnected by the LFDD
     scheme, with investigations ongoing into the cause for the remaining six. Two railway traction
     substations in the South of England were disrupted by the drop in frequency; they automatically switched
     to back-up generation with no impact on customer services.

PART 2 — HOSPITALS
H01  ESO section 5.3: Ipswich Hospital internal protection operated coincident with the timeframe of the
     lightning strike. Time-stamped data from UKPN shows that the hospital's load reduced by half in a period
     of 14 seconds [reported].
H02  ESO section 5.3: UKPN confirmed that the hospital was not part of its LFDD protection zone and that LFDD
     did not affect the substations supplying the hospital.
H03  ESO executive summary: impacts on other critical facilities included Ipswich hospital, which lost power
     due to the operation of its own protection systems.
H04  E3C interim report: a DNO confirmed that two hospitals were affected by LFDD, with their back-up
     generation working as designed. Another hospital was affected by the frequency fall and voltage excursion
     despite not being disconnected by LFDD; this was due to incorrect protection settings on the hospital's
     own network, which switched the site over to back-up generation, and one of its 11 [reported] generators
     failed to operate.
H05  E3C final report, section 4: four hospitals were impacted by the power outage; two were disconnected by
     the LFDD scheme and a further two by their internal safety systems. All hospitals automatically switched
     to back-up power supplies to ensure continued operation.
H06  Ofgem 2.11: two hospitals were disconnected as part of the LFDD and their back-up generators were
     activated; the E3C has reported that two other hospitals were disconnected by their own safety systems
     but switched to back-up generation.

PART 3 — AIRPORTS
A01  ESO section 5.3: Newcastle Airport is connected to the NPG network. NPG confirmed that the airport was
     disconnected as a result of the LFDD operation and that the LFDD scheme operated by NPG worked as
     planned; NPG is nonetheless reviewing all LFDD allocations. As far as NPG is aware, no Protected Sites
     under the Electricity Supply Emergency Code (ESEC) were affected by the incident.
A02  ESO section 5.3: Newcastle International Airport lost supplies from the network for 18 minutes [reported]
     between 16:53 [reported] and 17:11 [reported]. NPG indicated that the airport's Uninterruptable Power
     Supply (UPS) and standby generator resilience arrangements for its essential services operated smoothly.
A03  ESO section 5.3: on 12 August 2019 Northern Powergrid (Northeast) Limited received a request from
     Newcastle International Airport to be categorised as a Protected Site under ESEC, and it has now been
     registered as such.
A04  ESO executive summary: Newcastle airport was disconnected by the Low Frequency Demand Disconnection
     scheme.
A05  E3C interim report: DNOs confirmed that two airports, one in the Midlands and one in the north of
     England, were impacted. One was impacted as a result of LFDD stage 1 being automatically triggered; it
     had its own standby generation for its safety-critical systems, and power was restored via the
     distribution network after 17 minutes [reported]. The second, unaffected by LFDD, switched to back-up
     power supplies without issue and was restored within a few minutes; a fault with its on-site internal
     network meant that power to some services (check-in hall, central security search, hold baggage
     screening, and some telephony and comms systems) was delayed for up to 50 minutes [reported].
A06  E3C final report, section 4: Newcastle airport was disconnected from the electricity network following
     the LFDD and used back-up generation. The second airport was not impacted by the LFDD but switched to
     back-up power supplies and was restored within a few minutes; a fault with the on-site internal network
     disrupted some services, such as the check-in hall, for ~50 minutes [estimated].
A07  Ofgem 2.10: Newcastle airport was disconnected as part of LFDD; the E3C has reported that standby
     generation was in place and power was restored within minutes at Newcastle airport, and that a second
     airport switched to its back-up power supplies without issue although it was not affected by LFDD.

PART 4 — WATER
W01  E3C interim report: approximately 3,000 [estimated] people experienced water supply disruptions because
     booster water pumping stations failed to switch over automatically to back-up power supplies. Some would
     have had a temporary loss of running water at home, while others were unaffected because storage in the
     system allowed running water to continue; the majority of customers were restored within
     30 minutes [reported].
W02  E3C final report, section 4: the water sector experienced minimal impacts. Two water treatment works were
     disconnected, one through the LFDD scheme and one as a result of the company's internal safety systems.
     One water company reported a reduction in water pressure to 3000 [reported] customers because booster
     water pumping stations failed to switch automatically to back-up power; this was reduced to
     c.180 [estimated] customers within 30 minutes [reported].
W03  Ofgem 2.11: some water pumping stations were disconnected as part of the LFDD; the E3C has reported that
     their back-up supplies were not connected automatically and, as a result, several thousand customers
     experienced some disruption to their running water supply.

PART 5 — OIL REFINERY, CHEMICALS AND GAS
F01  E3C interim report: an oil refinery confirmed that it was disconnected as a result of the site's system,
     which detected a drop in frequency and disconnected the plant to protect on-site equipment. The refinery
     operations team used the site's emergency procedures and automated systems to shut down portions of the
     plant safely; because restarting large process units is complex, it took a few weeks to restore normal
     operations.
F02  E3C final report, section 4: wider industry reported the disconnection of an oil refinery and a chemicals
     manufacturing plant due to internal safety systems detecting the drop in frequency; to protect the assets
     both plants safely shut down operations, and it took several weeks for the refinery to resume full
     operations.
F03  E3C interim report: the gas networks and transmission operator reported that they implemented their
     response mitigation plans in a timely way.

PART 6 — ATTRIBUTED ANNOTATIONS ON ESSENTIAL SERVICES (statements made after the event)
N01  E3C final report, section 4: there is currently no agreed definition of what constitutes an essential
     service in this context; the report uses the term for organisations that rely on electricity to provide
     important daily services as well as critical industries, for example hospitals, airports, oil refineries
     and rail services.
N02  E3C final report, section 4: some essential services were disrupted by being disconnected directly
     through the LFDD mechanism; others by their automatic safety systems reacting unexpectedly to the
     frequency and voltage fluctuations, or by insufficient business continuity measures. Several sectors did
     not resume operations for several days.
N03  Ofgem 2.5: some essential service providers were directly disconnected as part of Stage 1 of the LFDD and
     disrupted because their back-up power supply arrangements were not effective; other services were
     affected indirectly because the providers' own safety systems were configured to disconnect automatically
     when system frequency fell.
N04  Ofgem 3.41 to 3.42: several essential service providers (such as hospitals and airports) were
     disconnected as part of LFDD; the LFDD equipment does not operate at an individual site level, so
     isolating particular sites is generally unfeasible. Ofgem states that disruptions at the sites of
     essential service providers directly affected were generally caused by failures in their back-up power
     arrangements, and that DNOs have significantly different approaches to evaluating which areas to
     disconnect during Stage 1 of the LFDD.

PART 7 — INDEX ENTRIES (written for this record; the indexed texts are not reproduced)
X01  Public statement on the website of East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Ipswich
     Hospital, dated 10 August 2019 [reported]: it describes a minor on-site power problem at the hospital;
     every standby generator operated, but one breaker serving outpatient services failed to, briefly
     interrupting electricity to outpatient and x-ray areas; business-continuity plans were invoked and the
     problem was resolved quickly, with other areas unaffected. The statement gives no times.
X02  Trade-press news item dated 12 September 2019 [reported] (Hydrocarbon Processing, credited to Reuters):
     it reports flaring at the Stanlow refinery when its grid electricity supply failed.

DOCUMENT S10 — Generator and network compliance-process records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO (compliance testing records, Appendix G, and answers to E3C questions);
Ofgem and E3C statements as attributed; roles only, no individuals
Record type: reconstructed compliance-process records with attributed regulator and E3C statements
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: no clock times are recorded; dates are UK calendar dates exactly as printed (dd/mm/yyyy or
dd.mm.yyyy in ESO's tables).
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the named source; [estimated] value the source gives as
approximate ("around"); [measured], [modelled], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
Dates, test names and code references are kept exactly as printed.

PART 1 — HORNSEA ONE COMPLIANCE RECORD (ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019, Appendix G "Compliance
Testing for Hornsea and Little Barford")
H01  NG ESO and Ørsted held 14 [reported] face to face operational notification connections compliance
     meetings between 21/03/2017 and 05/04/2019 to ensure that Ørsted fully understood the Grid Code
     requirements for a Hornsea offshore wind farm to demonstrate.
H02  Ørsted provided Grid Code requirement compliance data to NG ESO from 04/08/2017 to 21/06/2019; the first
     version of the fault ride through report was submitted on 30/04/2018. Following all the compliance data
     submissions, which included the simulation studies relating to Fault Ride Through, Voltage Control,
     Frequency Control and Reactive Capability demonstrating that Hornsea complies with the Grid Code through
     the design of the plant, NG ESO confirmed that the compliance data were satisfactory.
H03  Energisation of assets and synchronisation to the NETS (activity | date as printed):
C1   Energization of circuit 1 | 31/10/2018
C2   Energization of circuit 2 | 28/11/2018
C3   Synchronization of Reactive Compensators | 06/11/2018
C4   Synchronization of Module 1 | 15/07/2019
C5   Synchronization of Module 2 | 01/02/2019
C6   Synchronization of Module 3 | 30/04/2019
H04  Completed Grid Code compliance tests at 20% [reported] capacity, voltage tests (test | date of test |
     results sent to NG ESO | approval by ESO, as printed):
V1   Hornsea M1_20% Voltage test on Dynamic Reactive Compensator DRC10 | 15.01.2019 | 17.012019 | 17.012019
V2   Hornsea M2_20% Voltage test on Dynamic Reactive Compensator DRC20 | 15.01.2019 | 17.012019 | 17.012019
V3   Hornsea M3_20% Voltage test on Dynamic Reactive Compensator DRC30 | 15.01.2019 | 17.012019 | 17.012019
V4   Hornsea M1/2 20% [reported] Voltage test on Dynamic Reactive Compensators DRC10/20 together | 15.01.2019
     | 17.012019 | 17.012019
H05  Completed tests at 70% [reported] capacity, Limited Frequency sensitive Mode Tests OC5.A.3.3 (test | date
     of test | approval by ESO, as printed):
L1   Hornsea M2 70% [reported] Frequency test on High Performance Park Pilot (HPPP) 2 | 25.03.2019 |
     26.03.2019
L2   Hornsea M3 70% [reported] Frequency test on High Performance Park Pilot (HPPP) 2 | 07.06.2019 |
     13.06.2019
L3   Hornsea M1 70% [reported] Frequency test on High Performance Park Pilot (HPPP) 2 | 09.08.2019 |
     23.08.2019
H06  Completed Preliminary Frequency Response Tests OC5.A.3.6.4 (test | date of test | approval by ESO, as
     printed):
F1   Hornsea M2 Frequency tests on High Performance Park Pilot (HPPP) 2 | 25.03.2019 | 26.03.2019
F2   Hornsea M3 Frequency tests on High Performance Park Pilot (HPPP) 2 | 07.06.2019 | 13.06.2019
H07  List of outstanding tests: 70% [reported] capacity, Preliminary Frequency Response Tests on wind farm M1;
     100% [reported] capacity, Reactive Capability Testing on the 2 Transmission Interface Points CP.7.2.2(a),
     OC5.A.3.4; 100% [reported] capacity, Voltage Control Testing on the two connections CP.7.2.2(b),
     OC5.A.3.5; 100% [reported] capacity, Frequency Response Testing on the 3 Offshore Wind Farms CP.7.2.2(c)
     OC5.A.3.6.6.
H08  Further requirements outstanding before issuing the Final Operational Notification (FON): updates to
     documentation under CP.7.3, the most significant being model verification to demonstrate that the models
     and parameters reflect the test results (CP.7.3.1(c), CP.A.3.7), updated planning code data with the
     final commissioned status (CP.7.3.1(a)) and updated Compliance Statements (CP.7.3.1(e)).
H09  Ofgem report (dated 3 January 2020), 3.19: on 9 August two of Hornsea 1's modules were fully installed
     and the third was partially installed, so it had declared a total power export capability of
     800 MW [reported]. Hornsea 1 was progressing through the Grid Code compliance process and had fulfilled
     the necessary requirements to export on an interim basis.
H10  E3C final report (January 2020), chapter 1: at the time of the incident the windfarm was in the process
     of demonstrating compliance with the Grid Code before being allowed to export at maximum capacity; two of
     the units had passed the compliance tests, with the remaining unit permitted to export up to
     20% [reported] whilst awaiting further testing. These limits were granted by the ESO based on the testing
     and studies submitted at the time.

PART 2 — LITTLE BARFORD COMPLIANCE RECORD (ESO Appendix G)
B01  Little Barford connected to the transmission network in 1996, before the compliance process was included
     in the Grid Code; the compliance process applied to the replacement of the gas turbines and associated
     control systems.
B02  Compliance activities (activity | date as printed):
M1   ESO issued LON for Gas Turbine replacement | 06/01/2012
M2   Automatic Voltage Regulator & Power System Stabilizer Tests on GT1A | 07/01/2013
M3   Automatic Voltage Regulator & Power System Stabilizer Tests on GT1B | 17/01/2013
M4   Automatic Voltage Regulator & Power System Stabilizer Tests on ST10 | 01/10/2012
M5   Governor Tests | 15-19/03/2013
M6   ESO Issued FON | 26/04/2013
B03  Ofgem 3.25: Little Barford is a 740 MW [reported] combined cycle gas turbine power station owned and
     operated by RWE Generation and connected at the Eaton Socon 400 kV [reported] substation; its two gas
     turbines and one steam turbine were all operating on 9 August. It was commissioned in 1995 and went
     through a major upgrade in 2011/12.

PART 3 — ESO ANSWERS TO E3C QUESTIONS ON COMPLIANCE (Appendix M; based on the data available to the ESO on 28
August 2019)
Q01  Answer 43 (areas of concern about compliance testing with generators or OFTOs): after describing the
     compliance process, the ESO states: "We are not aware of concerns regarding the compliance testing
     process."
Q02  Answer 44: there have been no issues highlighted in the generation compliance process at Hornsea 1 or
     Little Barford in the past.
Q03  Answer 45: there are no direct tests of generator ride-through for faults and large or rapid frequency
     changes, which would require applying an intentional fault to the transmission system and could
     compromise its integrity. The asset owner performs simulation studies to demonstrate ride-through
     capability, and the ESO will not issue an Interim Operational Notice until it has reviewed these studies
     and determined that they are in line with Grid Code requirements.

PART 4 — OFGEM FINDINGS ON THE ESO'S COMPLIANCE CHECKS (Ofgem report, section 3 and executive summary)
G01  3.13: Ofgem has not found any evidence that the ESO failed to meet its requirements under the Grid Code
     in this area, and the ESO was not aware of any potential compliance issues with Hornsea 1 or Little
     Barford ahead of the event. However, the processes the ESO used to check their compliance do not appear
     sufficiently robust: the ESO relied significantly on self-certification by Hornsea 1 for the
     commissioning process as demonstration of its Grid Code compliance, despite the complexity of the
     connection, and after Little Barford's major refurbishment in 2011/12 relied on RWE's confirmation that
     the modifications had not affected compliance with the Grid Code requirements for generators to remain
     stable following network faults. No independent compliance testing or verification was carried out.
G02  3.14: Ofgem found limitations in the ESO's understanding of Hornsea 1's control system and of the
     interaction between its onshore and offshore arrangements, which impaired the ESO's view of Hornsea 1's
     performance after it was affected by the fault.
G03  3.15: the ESO allowed both Hornsea 1 and Little Barford to reconnect to the transmission system without
     taking adequate steps to determine the root cause of each failure. Hornsea 1 was reconnected and returned
     to service after the generator confirmed that the faulted equipment had been removed from service, but
     before the full root cause analysis had been completed, while it was still going through Grid Code
     compliance processes for commissioning generators.
G04  3.16: the Grid Code procedures the ESO is required to follow for checking generators' compliance may need
     to be clarified and strengthened; Ofgem expects the ESO to review the adequacy of the procedures it
     carries out and to flag potential compliance concerns to Ofgem.
G05  Executive summary: some licensees do not appear to have met their licence and code requirements, and the
     event highlights the importance of robust industry compliance processes. Ofgem has not identified any
     failures by the ESO to meet its requirements which contributed to the outage.

PART 5 — OFGEM FINDINGS ON PERFORMANCE AGAINST REQUIREMENTS (Ofgem report, section 3 and executive summary)
P01  Hornsea 1, 3.20: Hornsea 1's two fully operational modules deloaded automatically from around
     737 MW [estimated] to zero after the lightning strike, whilst its remaining module continued to generate
     at 62 MW [reported]; this occurred after the network fault on the Eaton Socon - Wymondley circuits had
     been rectified.
P02  Hornsea 1, 3.22: modelling that Ørsted carried out with its equipment manufacturer before 9 August
     suggested performance issues with the voltage control system with Hornsea 1 operating at its full planned
     1,200 MW [reported] capacity; these issues were not discussed with the ESO. The manufacturer proposed a
     software update, which Ørsted told Ofgem it had planned to carry out on 13 August but implemented on 10
     August, immediately after the event. The issue on 9 August occurred when the wind farm reached
     799 MW [reported]; prior simulations and discussions had not foreseen such issues at this capacity, nor
     that the wind farm would become unstable and de-load even at full load.
P03  Hornsea 1, 3.23: Hornsea 1 did not notify the ESO directly when the wind farm deloaded by
     737 MW [reported]. It then began starting up two of its modules (temporarily) without any coordination
     with the ESO, while the ESO was attempting to respond to the generation losses it was aware of.
P04  Hornsea 1, 3.24: the Grid Code requirements on generators' responses to network faults, known as Fault
     Ride Through requirements, require that generators remain connected and transiently stable following a
     fault on the transmission system, with power output recovering to at least 90% [reported] within
     0.5 seconds [reported] (Ofgem cites Connection Condition CC.6.3.15.1). Hornsea 1 has acknowledged that it
     did not meet this requirement, having deloaded following the fault. Hornsea 1 has also accepted that it
     did not meet the Grid Code requirement to have an overall voltage control system which appropriately
     dampens or limits swings (Ofgem cites CC.A.7.2.5.2, Voltage Control (Oscillations)).
P05  Little Barford, 3.26: Fault Ride Through requirements are fundamental to the security and resilience of
     the power system; Little Barford's generators did not continue providing power to the system following
     the lightning strike, and this contributed to the power outage.
P06  Little Barford, 3.28 to 3.29: the steam turbine tripped initially because of a discrepancy between its
     three independent speed sensors that exceeded the tolerance of the control system; the root cause of the
     discrepancy has not been established. One gas turbine was shut down automatically on excessive pressure
     in the steam bypass and the other was tripped manually by plant operators; the root cause of these high
     pressure conditions has not been established. Given the sequence of events and in the absence of an
     established root cause, Ofgem's preliminary view is that the steam turbine's anomalous speed readings and
     the resulting trip were due to the transmission network fault. RWE Generation has acknowledged the role
     it played in contributing to the power outage by not continuing to provide power to the system following
     the fault.
P07  DNOs, 3.36: most DNOs would appear to have met the Grid Code requirements regarding LFDD, but Ofgem found
     issues with essential services being disconnected, areas for improvement in the LFDD arrangements, and
     concerning evidence that some DNOs disconnected distributed generation via LFDD that was providing
     frequency response or reserve services. Most DNOs reconnected customers as required, but Ofgem found
     issues with two DNOs which could potentially have jeopardised the recovery of the system.
P08  DNOs, 3.43: DNOs' reconnection of demand following Stage 1 of LFDD generally performed as expected.
     However, Eastern Power Networks plc and South Eastern Power Networks plc (both owned by UK Power
     Networks) reconnected sites without being told to do so by the ESO, and acknowledge that they do not
     appear to have technically met the requirements of the Grid Code (Ofgem cites Grid Code Operation Code
     6.6.4). These instances were caused by the configuration of the DNOs' operational systems. The system
     frequency was successfully restored to 50 Hz [reported] following the LFDD activation; the premature
     demand reconnection could potentially have jeopardised this outcome.
P09  Executive summary: two DNOs (Eastern Power Networks plc and South Eastern Power Networks plc, owned by UK
     Power Networks) reconnected customers in England before the required instructions from the ESO, and this
     could have jeopardised recovery of the system.
P10  DNOs, 3.44: SP Distribution erroneously disconnected 22 MW [reported] in Scotland when system frequency
     fell below 48.8 Hz [reported] and reconnected customers without informing the ESO. As part of the SP
     Transmission network area it is not required by the Grid Code to disconnect demand until frequency
     reaches 48.5 Hz [reported]; the disconnection was due to an incorrect setting in its LFDD equipment.
     Since it was not responding to an LFDD event, Ofgem states that it does not appear to have contravened
     the Grid Code in its disconnection or prompt reconnection of demand without informing the ESO.
P11  NGET, 3.17 to 3.18: NGET's evidence shows fault clearance times for the two circuit breakers under
     75 ms [reported] and voltage remaining within a range of 390 kV [reported] to 410 kV [reported] following
     the fault; the evidence suggests that NGET's transmission assets performed as expected based on its Grid
     Code and SQSS requirements.
P12  Distributed generation, 3.31 to 3.32: some generators with capacities greater than 5 MW [reported] were
     reported to have de-loaded during the event, for reasons still to be determined precisely; their RoCoF
     protection settings should have been changed following Distribution Code modifications made in 2014. It
     is possible that the frequency protection settings on some generators were not changed in line with
     Distribution Code requirements.

DOCUMENT R09 — External communications records, 9-20 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO; Energy Emergencies Executive Committee (E3C); Ofgem;
Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS, GOV.UK); Elexon Limited (BMRS /
Insights REMIT data written by market participants); distribution network operators, train
operators and National Rail Enquiries (public posts and web pages)
Record type: report transcriptions and quotations on communications with government, the
regulator, the media and the public; real Elexon REMIT messages; times and short builder-written
gists of organisational public posts and web statements; Ofgem and GOV.UK publications quoted
STATUS: REAL DATA EXTRACTS WITH TRANSCRIBED REPORT TABLES — dataset values are unchanged from the
publishers' files (only rows and columns were selected); report tables, captions and quotations
are reproduced as printed. Nothing in Parts A-D and F is synthesised. Part E is not a
transcription: for each organisational post or web statement it gives the time (decoded, displayed
or titled) and a short gist written for this record; the text is not reproduced. Personal names
are replaced by roles in square brackets.
Clock reference: report times are printed without a zone; the reports give event times in local
time (BST, UTC+01:00). Elexon REMIT times are UTC (Z); the participants' free text may state BST.
Post times in Part E are UTC, decoded from the post identifiers; web statements carry a date and,
for some, a time in the page title (UK local time); archived web pages show times without a zone.
GOV.UK times carry explicit offsets.
Value-status legend: [measured] metered or observed value as published; [reported] value, time or
statement given by its publisher or by a report; [estimated] value its source describes as an
estimate; [modelled] value produced by a model; [digitised] and [illustrative] are not used.

PART A — ESO ACCOUNTS OF ITS CONTACTS WITH GOVERNMENT AND THE REGULATOR (quoted as printed)
A1   National Grid ESO, Technical Report on the events of 9 August 2019 (6 September 2019),
    section 6.2 'Engagement with government and the regulator', quoted:
    "The first communication between the ESO control room and BEIS was at 17:41hrs." [reported]
    "At this point the event was generally understood, demand restoration was in progress and
      further disturbances were considered unlikely." [reported]
    "The first communication with Ofgem was made at 17:51hrs with further communication at [reported]

DOCUMENT S06 — Embedded generation returns and published loss estimates, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Distribution Network Operators (returns to ESO); estimates by National Grid ESO, Ofgem
and the E3C as attributed below
Record type: reconstructed summary of the DNO embedded-generation return, its stated limits, and
published loss estimates listed by source, each with the source's own timing or stage words
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: times are hh:mm:ss as printed by ESO, with no clock labelled; read as BST (UTC+01:00)
because ESO dates the event at 4:52pm.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in a return or report; [estimated] value the source
calls an estimate or approximation; [modelled] value the source derives from frequency simulation or
modelling; [measured], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
No estimate below is a direct measurement of embedded generation output; each states its own basis.

PART 1 — DNO RETURNS TO THE ESO DATA REQUEST (as described in the ESO technical report dated
6 September 2019, section 4.2)
R1   After the event ESO contacted all DNOs and requested data on the volume of embedded generation that
     was disconnected or changed output during the event, and asked them to indicate the reason for the
     change of output, for example RoCoF, Vector Shift or Active Network Management (ANM) operation.
R2   All DNOs responded and indicated a combined total of 462 MW [reported] of embedded generation lost
     during the event.
R3   Some DNOs noted challenges in obtaining the data due to the way it is collected or stored. Without
     confirmation from generators, DNOs were unable to determine whether a specific generator tripped due
     to RoCoF or Vector Shift.
R4   A number of embedded generators and demand customers advised that their protection operated when
     the frequency reached 49 Hz [reported] and as such they were disconnected from the system.

PART 2 — LIMITS OF THE AVAILABLE DATA (as stated in the reports)
L1   ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M, data available on 28 August 2019): the majority of
     distribution connected generation provides no indication of proposed output, and no actual output
     data to the ESO.
L2   Ofgem 3.45: most DNOs only record information on generation volumes on their networks on a
     half-hourly basis, obscuring shorter-term events; the data DNOs provided gives only a partial view of
     which distributed generators tripped off or reduced output, so volumes lost at different locations
     and their causes cannot be ascertained with confidence from it.
L3   Ofgem 3.37: the information DNOs collect and record on distributed generation is variable or
     severely limited; the exact causes and timeline of the incident cannot be fully established.
L4   Ofgem, footnote 19: it has not been possible to fully validate the ESO estimate with the DNOs, as
     they also do not monitor output from distributed generators in real-time.
L5   Ofgem, footnote 31: Ofgem ascertained the distributed generation losses in section 2 of its report
     based on its validation of the frequency event modelling carried out by the ESO.

PART 3 — PUBLISHED ESTIMATES BY SOURCE (in each source's own words for timing, stage and basis; not
summed, grouped or reconciled)
ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019
E1   Table 1 (timeline): 16:52:33 [reported] approximately 150 MW [estimated] of embedded generation trips
     on vector-shift protection.
E2   Table 1 (timeline): 16:52:34 [reported] approximately 350 MW [estimated] of embedded generation trips
     on RoCoF protection [1,481MW cumulative infeed loss] [reported] (bracket as printed).
E3   Figure 2 annotation: increase in transformer loadings (Loss Of Mains) ~500 MW [estimated], labelled
     [16:52:34] [reported].
E4   Figure 2 annotation: embedded gen. loss 200 MW [modelled] @49Hz.
E5   section 4.2: post-event power system studies by ESO indicate that, for an event such as this, a loss
     of embedded generation on vector shift protection of approximately 150 MW [estimated] would be
     expected.
E6   section 4.2: based on the 150 MW [estimated] vector shift figure plus the data provided by the DNOs,
     approximately 350 MW [estimated] was lost due to RoCoF.
E7   section 4.2: a number of embedded generators and demand customers advised that their protection
     operated when the frequency reached 49 Hz [reported]; the net effect of this disconnection has been
     modelled as a 200 MW [modelled] loss of generation; protection operating at this frequency was not
     expected and has not previously been observed.
E8   footnote 2: ESO simulation data indicates that the overall total embedded generation loss could be
     slightly higher (580 MW [modelled] v 500 MW [estimated]).
E9   section 7: levels of embedded generation tripping due to RoCoF and vector shift were broadly in line
     with what was expected.
E10  section 8: during the event, approximately 500 MW [estimated] of embedded generation tripped on Loss
     of Mains protection (vector shift and Rate of Change of Frequency).
E11  Appendix I: the vector shift loss of 150 MW [estimated] is estimated to have occurred at the time of
     the circuit trip.
E12  Appendix I: based on the DNO data the RoCoF volume was 350 MW [estimated]; analysis of the simulation
     data indicates it may be slightly higher at 430 MW [modelled].
E13  Appendix I: modelling indicates that an additional 581 MW [modelled] of embedded generation was also
     disconnected, either part of the LFDD scheme or via another mechanism, resulting in a net reduction
     in demand of 350 MW [modelled].
ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M; data available on 28 August 2019)
E14  Answer 7: approximately 500 MW [estimated] of embedded generation was lost in the incident, estimated
     from the change in flows between the transmission and distribution networks in metered data from the
     ESO's IEMS system, corrected for the frequency characteristics of demand and for frequency response
     services in the distribution network; further analysis was to determine whether a split between RoCoF
     and vector shift could be made.
E3C interim report (October 2019)
E15  The ESO technical report states that approximately 600 MW [estimated] of embedded generation was also
     disconnected at this point, either as part of the LFDD scheme or via another mechanism, resulting in
     a net reduction in demand of 350 MW [reported].
Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020
E16  2.4.6: the frequency fell at a rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) above 0.125 Hz/s [reported]; some
     distributed generators have loss of mains protection triggered by RoCoF set at this rate; as a
     result, an estimated 350-430 MW [estimated] of distributed generation tripped off unnecessarily,
     based on information provided by the ESO.
E17  footnote 19 (to 2.4.6): this has been inferred by the ESO from a 500 MW [estimated] increase in
     transformer loadings at the interface with the distribution network; the ESO estimated
     150 MW [estimated] of vector shift and attributed the remainder to RoCoF; further ESO modelling
     suggests the total from vector shift and RoCoF could have been up to 580 MW [modelled].
E18  2.4.11 and footnote 20: there was a further net reduction in generation of 200 MW [reported] at
     49 Hz [reported]; some distributed generators tripped due to protection set to activate when the
     frequency falls to 49 Hz [reported], which could be the cause; the figure is net of demand
     disconnection, such as trains and large industrial customers.
E19  2.4.12-2.4.13: after system frequency dropped below 48.8 Hz [reported], triggering Stage 1 of LFDD,
     the ESO reported that the net demand reduction seen by the transmission system was only
     350 MW [reported]; this indicates that approximately 550 MW [estimated] of additional distributed
     generation was lost at this point.
E20  3.30: lower bound for total estimated distributed generation lost across the event is
     1,300 MW [estimated], and the loss could be as high as 1,500 MW [estimated].
E21  3.31: at least 500 MW [estimated] of distributed generation is estimated to have been lost due to
     loss of mains protection settings (RoCoF and vector shift) in the first second after the fault; some
     generators with capacities greater than 5 MW [reported] were reported to have de-loaded during the
     event and the cause is still to be determined precisely.
E22  3.32 and footnote 27: in excess of 200 MW [reported] of distributed generation tripped off when
     system frequency reached 49 Hz [reported]; significantly more may have tripped at this point, as the
     modelling is net of demand that was simultaneously disconnected such as the trains.
E3C final report (January 2020)
E23  section 1: five significant modes of embedded generator loss: vector shift, which disconnected
     approximately 150 MW [estimated]; RoCoF protection, which disconnected between 350-430 MW [reported];
     embedded generation shutting down at a frequency of 49 Hz [reported], not expected, resulting in a
     further net reduction of 200 MW [reported]; an unexpected increase in electricity demand in parallel
     with the loss of generation, attributed to the de-loading or tripping of 100 MW [reported] of
     embedded generation, the cause unknown at present; and the final loss, as reported in the ESO
     technical report, of 550 MW [reported], when the LFDD scheme was triggered. In total across the
     event, the loss of embedded generation is estimated to be in the range of
     1300 MW to 1500 MW [estimated].

findings.statement: A single blue-phase-to-earth fault on one Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV circuit started at 16:52:33.490 BST, about 4.5 km from Wymondley Main. MeteoGroup recorded three almost simultaneous lightning strikes near the circuit at 16:52:33, the largest 33.7 kA, and NGET attributes the fault to lightning.

Main protection cleared the fault in 70 ms at Wymondley Main and 74 ms at Eaton Socon, inside the 80 ms required at 400 kV under CC.6.2.3.1.1. NGET and Ofgem assess that the transmission assets performed as expected.
The circuit was re-energised by delayed auto-reclose at 16:52:53 BST, about 20 s after the fault. No defects were found at the substations or on the 10 August line inspection.

No compliance concern is raised against NGET: clearance times and post-fault voltages were within the cited limits. Two other lightning trips that day, Harker–Stella West and Blyth–Eccles–Stella West, reclosed with no losses, although the record gives two different times for the Blyth trip.

Hornsea 1B and 1C de-loaded between 16:52:33.728 and 16:52:33.835 BST (the log shows 15:52Z), leaving 1A at 62 MW: a 737 MW loss as reported by the ESO and Ofgem. Ørsted attributes it to the wind farm control system responding to an insufficiently damped sub-synchronous resonance triggered by the fault, which led to overcurrent protection on the turbines.

quantity.basis: reported sum of the three units

findings.statement: At Little Barford, ST1C tripped about 1.16 s after datum T (T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s, clock not stated, read as BST), losing 244 MW. GT1A tripped automatically at T + 57.6 s (210 MW) and GT1B was tripped manually at T + 84.6 s (187 MW), a station total of 641 MW. All figures are reported.

Ørsted had identified voltage-control issues at 1,200 MW in modelling but did not discuss them with the ESO. A damped oscillation occurred about 10 minutes before the event. A software fix planned for 13 August was applied on 10 August. Hornsea acknowledges it did not meet the fault ride through requirement (CC.6.3.15.1) or the voltage-control oscillation requirement (CC.A.7.2.5.2).

The ESO estimates about 150 MW of embedded generation tripped on vector-shift protection at the fault and about 350 MW on RoCoF protection at about 16:52:34 (430 MW in its model). These figures are inferred from about 500 MW of increased transformer loadings, not measured. The DNOs' combined return was 462 MW.

The 1-s frequency record shows a fall of 0.151 Hz between 16:52:34 and 16:52:35, which exceeds the 0.125 Hz/s RoCoF setting. This is consistent with RoCoF loss-of-mains trips, although 1-s differencing cannot resolve the instantaneous RoCoF.
The losses in the first second, on the ESO's cumulative basis of Hornsea, ST1C, vector shift and RoCoF, totalled 1,481 MW, against a secured loss of 1,000 MW.

quantity.basis: reported, ESO cumulative over the whole event

findings.statement: The ESO's cumulative total including GT1A and GT1B is 1,878 MW. ESO Appendix H counts the secured-event losses as 1,528 MW (737 + 641 + 150), plus about 350 MW of RoCoF trips.
Other totals: Ofgem gives at least 1,990 MW cumulative, including a 200 MW net loss at 49 Hz. The E3C gives about 2,100 MW (interim) and at least 2,000 MW (final).

Ofgem and the E3C estimate total embedded-generation loss across the event at 1,300–1,500 MW. This includes about 550 MW (Ofgem; 581 MW modelled by the ESO) lost when LFDD operated, leaving a net demand reduction of only about 350 MW.
The measured frequency was about 50.0 Hz before the event and fell to a first minimum of 49.083 Hz at 16:52:59 BST. It recovered to about 49.27 Hz by 16:53:17 and fell again after GT1A tripped.

findings.derivation: minimum of the R01 series after 16:52:33
findings.statement: The overall minimum in the measured record was 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49 BST (row 830). Reports round this to 48.8 Hz.

findings.derivation: count of samples with f < 49.0 Hz; the run is contiguous
findings.statement: Frequency was below 49.0 Hz in 33 consecutive 1-s samples, from 16:53:41 to 16:54:13 BST, i.e. about 33 s (±1 s from the sampling). This matches ORR's approximately 33 s and contradicts GTR's 16 s. The minima between samples are not resolved.

After the minimum, frequency first reached 50 Hz at 16:57:16 BST (50.001 Hz, row 1037), about 3 min 27 s after the minimum. The ESO gives 16:57:15. Frequency regained 49.5 Hz at 16:55:00 and later overshot to 50.248 Hz at 17:00:42.
The ESO was securing for a 1,000 MW loss and held 1,022 MW of primary and 1,314 MW of secondary low-frequency response (Table 3). Its earlier answer gives 1,338 MW of secondary.

Of the validated holding, 89% of primary (841 MW) and 88% of secondary (1,055 MW) performed as expected. About 1,090 MW was delivered within 30 s, excluding the demand effect. Ofgem reports under-delivery of 17% (primary) and 14% (secondary), and about 25% for mandatory and FFR providers.
Inertia was not measured but estimated: 210 GVA.s in ESO Table 4 and 219,632 MVA.s immediately before the trip in ESO answer 42. The NESO dataset gives 206 for period 36 (no unit stated).

The losses of about 1,481 MW in the first second, and 1,878 MW or more in total, exceeded the 1,000 MW secured and the response held. Recovery depended on LFDD and on 1,240 MW of control-room actions (STOR, Dinorwig/Ffestiniog, Coryton, Carrington). Ofgem judged that better response delivery would not have prevented demand disconnection.
Stage 1 LFDD (48.8 Hz trigger) operated as frequency reached its minimum at about 16:53:49 BST. The Elexon DCI record shows a 931 MW demand control event from 15:54Z to 16:40Z (16:54–17:40 BST).

Demand disconnected by LFDD: 931 MW and 1,152,878 customers (ESO Table 6, DNO data as of 13 August; 3.2% of 29 GW). The E3C table totals 973 MW, with WPD West Midlands at 190 MW and WPD South West at 12 MW. Ofgem gives 892 MW of net demand. The ESO says LFDD provided slightly under the 5% stage-1 design.
The ESO received the first DNO report at 16:56 BST. It began instructing restoration at 16:58 (UKPN LPN) and had issued all instructions by 17:16. The earlier ESO account gives 17:00–17:19.

Disconnected demand was restored by 17:37 BST according to ESO Tables 6 and 7, with the earliest area at 17:07. Other ESO sources give about 17:40 and 'by 18:30' (statement of 9 August, 8pm), and GOV.UK says 'within 90 minutes'. This is the restoration of demand, separate from the recovery of other services.

Under OC6.6 DNOs may not restore LFDD demand without ESO instruction. UKPN's EPN and SPN reconnected sites before instruction and acknowledge they did not technically meet OC6.6.4; ESO Table 6 shows UKPN Eastern fully restored at 16:56, before the EPN instruction at 17:14. SP Distribution disconnected 22 MW because of a wrong setting. This is a demonstrated, acknowledged non-conformity, but the feeder-level times are not held.

GTR's Class 700 and 717 trains shut down their 4QC converter protectively when supply frequency fell below 49 Hz (Siemens designed to EN 50163's 49 Hz note, although the specification claimed operation down to 48.5 Hz). Traction power was not lost.

Units on TCMS software 3.27 went into a permanent lockout that a battery reset could not clear, so a technician with a laptop was needed. Counts differ: GTR says about 60 shut down, 27/28 were recovered by drivers and about 30 needed technicians; ORR and Ofgem say 29 locked out (22 permanent, 7 reset), with 31 trains stranded and 30 evacuated. GTR reports 23 evacuations.

Reported scale of rail disruption: 371 trains cancelled, 220 part-cancelled and 873 delayed, with 14,428 delay minutes (ORR, from Network Rail's daily report). St Pancras and King's Cross closed for hours. Separately, my count of Network Rail TRUST records for 31 selected incidents gives 10,033 delay minutes on GTR Class 700 incidents and 8,248 on 'National Grid' incidents.

Rail recovery: Thameslink ran no service north of London for the rest of 9 August, disruption continued into 10 August because trains and crews were out of position, and ORR reports full service restored within 24 hours. The E3C says delays extended into 11 August.

Other rail and transport effects: Merseyrail Wirral line traction was lost through SP's LFDD (428 delay minutes); eight rural signalling supplies were lost (two through LFDD, six under investigation); the Victoria line was suspended by an internal traction issue and restored at 17:35.

Hospitals: two were disconnected by LFDD and two by their own protection, and all switched to back-up. At Ipswich Hospital (not in an LFDD zone) internal protection operated and one breaker or generator failed. Accounts differ (ESO, E3C, Trust) and no site electrical records are held.

Newcastle Airport was disconnected by LFDD from 16:53 to 17:11 (18 min, NPG/ESO) and registered as an ESEC Protected Site on 12 August. A second airport had a fault on its internal network lasting up to about 50 min. About 3,000 water customers were affected when booster pumps failed to switch to back-up. A refinery took weeks to restore operations. The Grid Code gives essential services no LFDD protection.

The ESO's first contact with BEIS was at 17:41 BST (section 6.2), or 17:40 (section 7). The first contact with Ofgem was at 17:51 (section 6.2), 18:00 (section 7) or 'just after 18:00' (answer 34). The ENCC reported to the Head of National Control at 17:10. ESO procedure calls for notification as soon as possible.

The ESO's first public statement was posted at 17:27:46Z (18:27 BST), once DNOs had reconnected customers. Clock basis: BST (UTC+01:00) throughout. Times printed in reports without a zone are read as BST because the ESO dates the event 4:52pm. Elexon, REMIT and decoded social-post times are UTC (Z), and I added 1 h to convert them. R01 is native BST (+01:00).

- 16:52:33.490: lightning fault on the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit. It was cleared at .560 and .564, and the circuit reclosed on DAR at 16:52:53 [F01, F02, F03].
- 16:52:33.728–.835: Hornsea 1B/1C de-load 737 MW. The S01 log is in UTC, 15:52Z [F05].
- About 16:52:34: Little Barford ST1C trips (244 MW). The station's datum T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s, on an unstated clock. Embedded-generation loss-of-mains trips occur at about the same time [F06, F08].
- 16:52:59: first frequency minimum of 49.083 Hz (R01). The ESO prints 49.1 Hz at 16:52:58 [F14].
- About 16:53:31: GT1A trips (T + 57.62 s) [F06].
- 16:53:41–16:54:13: frequency below 49 Hz. 16:53:49: minimum of 48.787 Hz, and stage 1 LFDD operates [F15, F16, F22].
- About 16:53:58: GT1B tripped manually (T + 84.6 s) [F06].
- 16:57:16: frequency first reaches 50 Hz. The ESO gives 16:57:15 [F17].
- 16:56: first DNO report to the ESO. 16:58–17:16: restoration instructions issued. 17:37: restoration complete (ESO) [F24, F25].
- 17:40/17:41: ESO contacts BEIS. 17:51 or 18:00: ESO contacts Ofgem. 18:27: first ESO public statement [F34, F35].

sections.heading: Consequences

sections.body:
**Disagreements between sources:**
- Generation totals: ESO, Ofgem and E3C [F11, F12, F13].
- LFDD volume: 931 vs 973 vs 892 MW [F23].
- Restoration time: 17:37, 17:40, 18:30 [F25].
- Train counts and the time below 49 Hz: 16 s per GTR vs about 33 s per ORR and R01 [F28, F29].
- Inertia: 210 GVA.s vs 219,632 MVA.s [F20].
- BEIS and Ofgem contact times [F34].

**Limits of measurement:** R01 is sampled at 1 s, so sub-second minima and RoCoF are not resolved [F14, F16]. No embedded generation is metered in real time [F40]. The Little Barford SOE clock is not aligned with the ESO's [F06].

**Unresolved causes:** the Little Barford speed-signal discrepancy and bypass-pressure excursions [F39]; the 100 MW drift and the 49 Hz trips [F41]; the volume of embedded generation lost at the LFDD stage [F13].
sections.heading: Uncertainties

sections.body:
1. **Ørsted** to provide controller logs and model revalidation to the ESO. Verify through ESO acceptance of the revalidated models and FON tests [F05, F07, F37].
2. **RWE** to report the root causes found by the bypass inspection and ST speed-sensor investigation. Verify with the inspection report and OEM test results [F06, F39].
3. **ESO** to review its security policy for coincident embedded-generation and transmission losses, and to strengthen compliance verification. Verify through a published policy change and audit [F11, F21, F38].
4. **DNOs and the Distribution Code administrator** to complete the loss-of-mains protection changes and provide sub-half-hourly embedded-generation data. Verify through programme completion statistics [F08, F40].
5. **UKPN** to correct the system configuration that allowed automatic reconnection. Verify through a test witnessed by the ESO [F26].
6. **Siemens and GTR** to roll out the auto-recovery patch and consider ride-through to 48.5 Hz. Verify through fleet software records [F28].
7. **Essential-service operators** to test their back-up supplies. Verify with test records [F31, F32, F33].
8. **ESO, DNOs and rail operators** to agree joint communication protocols. Verify by exercise [F35, F36].
sections.heading: Recommendations

sections.body:
**Requests:**
- **Ørsted:** turbine-controller logs (not held) [F07].
- **RWE:** plant instrumentation and control records (not held) [F39].
- **DNOs:** feeder-level LFDD relay logs (not held) and reconnection switching records [F22, F26].
- **DNOs:** real-time embedded-generation telemetry [F40].
- **ESO:** PMU/WAMS traces to resolve sub-second frequency and RoCoF [F16].
- **ESO:** control-room communications log, to confirm the BEIS and Ofgem contact times [F34].
- **GTR:** on-board TCMS logs [F28].

**Notification and coordination required by the evidence:**
- Grid Code OC6.6: DNOs must notify the ESO of LFDD operation and must not restore without its instruction [F26].
- ESO procedure: notify Ofgem and BEIS as soon as possible [F34].
- Generators must notify the ESO of changes affecting compliance [F37].
